content: 1. Gonorrhea is the most frequently reported communicable disease in the United States. 2. Disseminated gonococcal infection is the leading cause of acute septic arthritis in sexually active adults and accounts for the majority of hospitalizations due to infectious arthritis. 3. This male patient presented with purulent penile discharge caused by gonorrhea, accompanied by an overlying penile pyodermal lesion. 4. Pyoderma involves the formation of a purulent skin lesion, which in this case was located on the glans penis and overlaid the sexually transmitted infection gonorrhea. 5. This patient presented with symptoms later diagnosed as gonococcal pharyngitis. 6. Gonococcal pharyngitis is a sexually transmitted infection acquired through oral sex with an infected partner. 7. Most throat infections caused by gonococci are asymptomatic, but some individuals may experience mild to severe sore throat. 8. When collecting a specimen from a male suspected of having gonorrhea, if no discharge is evident, the urethra is stripped towards the orifice to express pus. 9. A thin sterile swab is then inserted approximately 2-3 cm into the urethra, rotated, and withdrawn for testing. 10. This patient presented with gonorrheal ecthyma on the skin, caused by systemically disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae bacteria. 11. Ecthyma is a cutaneous eruption characterized by a large, round pustule on an inflamed base, caused by untreated gonococcal bacteria spreading systemically through the bloodstream. 12. Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, if left untreated, can enter the bloodstream and disseminate throughout the body. 13. Systemic dissemination of gonorrhea may manifest as skin lesions throughout the body. 14. This newborn presented with gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, caused by a maternally transmitted gonococcal infection. 15. 16. This condition affects the corneal epithelium, leading to microbial keratitis, ulceration, and potential perforation. 17. This patient with diagnosed gonococcal urethritis presented with unilateral gonococcal conjunctivitis. 18. If untreated, Neisseria gonorrhoeae bacteria may spread to the bloodstream and throughout the body, causing symptoms such as rash, joint pain, and conjunctivitis. 19. This patient presented with gonorrhea and a disseminated gonococcal skin infection around the ankle. 20. Disseminated gonococcal infection is often associated with systemic symptoms, including skin lesions and joint pain. 21. This photograph shows a skin lesion on a patient diagnosed with gonorrhea, caused by the systemic spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. 22. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus and the causative agent of gonorrhea. 23. These bacteria can infect the genital tract, mouth, and rectum, and may disseminate throughout the bloodstream. 24. This is a close-up of a gonococcal lesion on the skin of a patient’s arm. 25. Full systemic dissemination of gonorrhea may manifest as skin lesions in the form of gray pustules. 26. This is a photograph of a skin lesion in a patient with systemically disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae bacteria. 27. This technician is about to collect an intraurethral specimen to test for gonorrhea or non-specific urethritis. 28. Physicians and healthcare workers typically use three laboratory techniques to diagnose gonorrhea: direct staining of samples for the bacterium, detection of bacterial genes or DNA in urine, and growing the bacteria in laboratory cultures. 29. This photomicrograph depicts a dorsal view of an adult female human head louse, Pediculus humanus capitis. 30. Lice are parasitic insects that can be found on people’s heads, bodies, and pubic areas. 31. Human lice survive by feeding on human blood. 32. Lice found on different areas of the body are distinct from one another. 33. The three types of lice that live on humans are Pediculus humanus capitis (head louse), Pediculus humanus corporis (body louse or clothes louse), and Pthirus pubis (crab louse or pubic louse). 34. Only the body louse is known to spread disease. 35. Lice infestations are most commonly spread through close person-to-person contact. 36. Dogs, cats, and other pets do not play a role in the transmission of human lice. 37. Lice move by crawling; they cannot hop or fly. 38. Both over-the-counter and prescription medications are available for the treatment of lice infestations.
